qs.q: Which group is most likely to develop severe disease from cytomegalovirus?
qs.e: Congenital CMV in newborns causes serious sequelae such as hearing loss and microcephaly. Other groups usually experience milder illness.

qs.q: An HIV-positive patient receiving ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis requires careful monitoring of which laboratory parameter due to a known major adverse effect?
o: Full blood count for bone marrow suppression
Serum troponin for negative inotropic effects
Visual acuity for permanent lens clouding
Liver function tests for isolated cholestasis
qs.e: Ganciclovir frequently causes bone marrow suppression, manifesting as neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, necessitating weekly full blood counts. It does not cause negative inotropic effects like certain azoles.

qs.q: Which glycoprotein serves as the major fusion protein required for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) entry into all host cell types?
qs.e: gB (UL55) is identified as the major fusion protein required for CMV entry into all cell types. The gM/gN complex is essential for viral replication, and the gH/gL/gO complex assists in cell-to-cell spread.
qs.s: Herpesviridae: HSV-1, HSV-2 Pathogenesis & Clinical Diseases: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with systemic cytomegalovirus infection is prescribed an antiviral agent. Which mechanism of action characterizes drugs effective against Cytomegalovirus?
o: Blocking viral uncoating via M2 channels
qs.e: Antiviral drugs acting by inhibition of viral DNA polymerase are effective against Cytomegalovirus. RNA viruses such as influenza, measles, mumps, and rabies do not respond to viral DNA polymerase inhibitors.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: A pregnant woman contracts cytomegalovirus. Which route is responsible for the newborn’s infection?
qs.e: CMV crosses the placenta to cause congenital infection. The other routes transmit infection after birth, not congenitally.
qs.s: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Guide: Pathogenesis, Dx & Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: What type of mononucleosis is characteristically caused by Cytomegalovirus (CMV)?
qs.e: Cytomegalovirus classically causes heterophile-negative mononucleosis, distinguishing it from Epstein-Barr virus which causes heterophile-positive infectious mononucleosis. Picornaviruses are unrelated to mononucleosis syndromes.
qs.s: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Guide: Pathogenesis, Dx & Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: Which safety measure in blood processing involves reducing white blood cells to help prevent febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions and cytomegalovirus transmission?
qs.e: Leucodepletion reduces white blood cells to prevent febrile non-haemolytic reactions, CMV transmission, and HLA alloimmunisation. Irradiation instead targets viable donor lymphocytes to prevent graft-versus-host disease.
qs.s: Blood Transfusion Guide: ABO, Reactions, Products & Safety: MCQs

qs.q: What is the key histological feature found in cytomegalovirus (CMV) infected cells when observed under a microscope?
qs.e: CMV histology is characterized by multinucleated giant cells with owl's eye intranuclear inclusion bodies. Downey cells are atypical lymphocytes seen in EBV infection.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: CMV is a ubiquitous herpesvirus that establishes lifelong latency and can reactivate in immunosuppressed hosts, causing severe disease especially in neonates and transplant recipients. Clinical reasoning hinges on recognizing risk factors, interpreting virology tests, and balancing antiviral therapy with toxicity.

sections.p: CMV is a double‑stranded DNA virus of the Herpesviridae family. It is widespread, often asymptomatic, but can cause life‑threatening disease when immunity wanes or in utero.
b: Latency in monocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells

sections.p: The virus has a large genome encoding proteins that modulate host immunity. It enters cells via glycoprotein complexes and replicates in the nucleus.
CMV spreads by direct contact with saliva, urine, blood, breast milk, or organ transplantation. After primary infection, it establishes latency and may reactivate.
b: Vertical transmission via placenta or breast milk

sections.p: In immunocompetent adults, CMV is usually mild or asymptomatic. In neonates, transplant recipients, and HIV patients, it can cause retinitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, and encephalitis.
b: Congenital CMV: sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, chorioretinitis

sections.p: Diagnosis relies on serology, PCR, and antigen detection. Clinical context guides interpretation.
Antiviral therapy is the cornerstone; valganciclovir or ganciclovir are first line. Supportive care and monitoring of marrow suppression are essential.

Remember that CMV is the most common congenital viral infection and that retinitis is a sight‑threatening complication in AIDS. In transplant patients, prophylaxis with valganciclovir reduces CMV disease.
b: CMV retinitis presents with floaters, blurred vision; treat promptly.

sections.p: HSV and EBV share latency and reactivation patterns but differ in organ tropism and treatment.
b: HSV: skin lesions, encephalitis; treat with acyclovir.

sections.p: IgM can persist long after infection; low PCR in early disease may miss active infection.
b: IgG avidity needed to confirm recent infection.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe visual loss, sudden hearing loss, respiratory distress, or unexplained fever in immunocompromised patients

faq.q: Can CMV be transmitted by casual contact?
faq.a: Yes, through saliva or urine; hand hygiene reduces risk.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for CMV?
faq.a: No licensed vaccine yet; research is ongoing.
